name: White root rot
summary: A pathogenicity-confirmed hemp root disease reported from one commercial field in southern Italy. The useful visual pattern combines plant-linked canopy decline with white root-surface mycelium and fan-like sub-bark growth, but neither wilt nor white fungal material identifies the pathogen without laboratory confirmation.
affectedParts: root crown and soil immediately over infected roots
field distribution and neighboring root zones
indicators: The same intact hemp plant shows canopy yellowing or apical wilt together with compatible root rot and white mycelium; canopy-only and detached-root observations remain unlinked evidence.
Conspicuous white mycelium covers affected hemp roots in the primary report, while cross-crop institutional guidance describes scattered cobwebby webs or strands on roots and nearby soil.
Carefully lifting the cortex or bark at an active root lesion reveals white, fluffy, fan-like mycelial growth rather than relying only on growth on the exposed outer surface.
White-to-greyish mycelial mats and progressively rotten tissue are useful cross-crop capture cues, but color and texture must not be treated as Cannabis-specific or species-diagnostic.

Older Rosellinia mycelium can darken to tan, brown, or blackish and become crustlike on dead roots, so capture both the living lesion margin and dead center rather than requiring bright white growth at every stage.

In the single Campania outbreak, visible yellowing and apical wilt preceded death by about two to three weeks and about 10% of plants were affected; neither value is a universal progression clock, prevalence estimate, or severity threshold.

A high-value image set links the whole plant and field position to crown, unwashed root system, white surface growth, lifted-cortex interface, lesion margin, and a healthy comparison under neutral light with a metric scale.
A confirmed label requires compatible isolation and morphology plus validated molecular identification from plant-linked root tissue; visual agreement alone is at most a low-confidence suspect label.
exclusions: White growth is present only on dead debris, the container surface, or detached roots without an intact plant and active lesion margin, supporting saprophytic colonization or contamination rather than confirmed disease.
Cottony growth at the soil line with round white, tan, or brown sclerotia supports southern blight and requires its own laboratory workup.
White stem or crown growth with hard black sclerotia within or on affected tissue supports the Sclerotinia white-mold/crown-rot complex.
Water-soaked, brown, sloughing roots in a saturated root zone without white sub-bark mycelium support Pythium or Phytophthora investigation, which must be resolved by oomycete-directed testing.
Brown cortical lesions or damping-off without compatible white sub-bark growth support Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, or another root/crown pathogen and require culture or molecular differential testing.
Large coherent sub-bark fans, mushroomlike odor, rhizomorphs, or basidiocarps support an Armillaria differential; the cited distinction is cross-crop and still requires expert confirmation.

White granules, salt crust, perlite, root hairs, mycorrhizae, insect wax, or a beneficial inoculant remain material or organism confounders unless microscopy and plant-linked sampling demonstrate invasive Rosellinia.
Measured drought, hypoxia, salinity/high EC, pH injury, root restriction, or nematodes adequately explain decline and representative living lesion margins are negative for the pathogen.

progression.description: Contaminated roots, root debris, soil, runoff, or planting material may precede visible disease; history alone is risk context and never a positive label.
White cobwebby strands, webs, or a mat may become visible on infected roots or adjacent soil; record its exact attachment before cleaning or incubation.
Root tissue rots and lifting cortex at the active margin can reveal a white fluffy or fan-like layer; older growth may darken and become crustlike.
Yellowing and apical wilt develop while compatible root signs remain on the same plant; canopy morphology is nonspecific and must stay linked to the root sequence.

Plants in the one reported hemp outbreak could die about two to three weeks after symptoms appeared, but cultivar, site, inoculum, and environment prevent transfer of that timing as a universal threshold.

lookAlikes: Sclerotinia white mold / crown rot complex
Saprophytic white mold on dead roots or substrate
Trichoderma or another introduced beneficial fungus
Perlite, mineral residue, or salt crust
Root aphid wax or mealybug residue
confirmation: Do not confirm white root rot from a canopy image, white material alone, or a detached root. Cap image/video-only confidence at 0.20 and route every organism-level proposal to human review.

Capture an uninterrupted plant-linked sequence before cleaning: field or bench position, whole canopy, crown, entire unwashed root system, white growth attachment, both sides of a lifted-cortex interface, and active lesion margin with scale and neutral color reference.

Sample multiple fresh living-to-necrotic root margins and sub-bark interfaces, plus a comparable healthy plant; avoid relying on decomposed centers or material incubated without documenting its original attachment.

Record plant age and cultivar, onset and repeat dates, neighboring-plant pattern, prior crop or perennial-root history, planting-stock source, root-debris and soil movement, irrigation/runoff, substrate, root-zone temperature, moisture, pH, and EC.

Submit plant-linked tissue to a qualified plant-diagnostic laboratory for isolation and morphology plus a validated molecular assay; preserve the chain between sample, image, culture, sequence result, and plant identifier.

Request a differential workup for southern blight, Sclerotinia, Pythium/Phytophthora, Fusarium, Rhizoctonia, Armillaria where plausible, and pair pathogen testing with root-zone measurements and nematode assessment.

Use serial imaging to document change but not to prove identity. Keep canopy-only, detached-root, white-growth-only, incubation-only, culture-unlinked, single-locus-ambiguous, mixed-pathogen, low-resolution, cross-crop, stock, generated, vendor, forum, anecdotal, or rights-unclear samples out of confirmed ground truth.
immediateActions: Isolate affected root-zone soil, tools, footwear, water runoff, and root debris from clean production areas while preserving representative plant-linked samples.
Photograph and sample before uprooting or washing; mark neighboring plants and inspect their root zones without spreading soil.
Contact a qualified plant-diagnostic laboratory and follow local plant-health reporting or containment requirements before moving suspect plants or substrate.
correctivePlan: Base culling, sanitation, soil/root-zone handling, and any crop-protection decision on confirmed disease and options currently legal for hemp in the jurisdiction.
Remove or contain infected roots and debris only under locally appropriate biosecurity guidance, and prevent contaminated soil or runoff from reaching clean production zones.
Track marked neighboring plants and reopen the differential if laboratory results, progression, or root-zone measurements conflict with the proposed diagnosis.
prevention: Use documented pathogen-free planting material and inspect roots before introduction where lawful and practical.
Avoid moving soil, water, tools, containers, or persistent root debris from confirmed areas into clean production zones.
Maintain drainage and irrigation records and inspect sites with susceptible perennial-crop history or unexplained root-rot mortality without assuming that history proves current infection.
warnings: The direct Cannabis evidence is one pathogenicity-confirmed commercial-field report from Campania; its approximately 10% incidence and two-to-three-week decline are site-specific observations.

UC IPM and Agriculture Victoria provide non-Cannabis morphology and biosecurity context. Their woody-host symptoms, timing, climate associations, host outcomes, and management claims are not Cannabis thresholds.

Rosellinia/Dematophora taxonomy, white mycelium, and fan-like sub-bark growth do not make images species-resolving; mixed infections and multiple white-growth look-alikes require laboratory exclusion.

The Agriculture Victoria figures are credited to the State of Queensland and lack verified item-level automated-training rights. No media file was copied or indexed, and this profile intentionally remains an explicit licensed-image and video gap.

Human review is mandatory for canopy-only, detached-root, white-growth-only, incubation-only, morphology-only, culture-unlinked, molecularly ambiguous, mixed-pathogen, cross-crop, low-resolution, generated, vendor, forum, anecdotal, or rights-unclear samples.

sources.title: First Report of White Root Rot of Hemp (Cannabis sativa) Caused by Dematophora necatrix in Campania Region (Southern Italy)
supportedClaims: Affected hemp developed yellowing, apical wilt, root rot, white mycelium covering roots, and fan-like mycelium beneath root bark before death.

In the single reported commercial field in Campania, death generally occurred within two to three weeks after first symptoms and about 10% of plants were affected; these are outbreak observations, not universal Cannabis timing or prevalence.
Inoculated hemp reproduced chlorosis, apical wilt, and death while controls remained healthy; the fungus was reisolated and confirmed by morphology and molecular analysis.
Root signs and laboratory confirmation are required because canopy yellowing and wilt overlap many Cannabis root-zone disorders.

sources.title: Dematophora Root Rot, or Rosellinia Root Rot
sources.organization: University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program
sources.publisher: Regents of the University of California, Agriculture and Natural Resources
supportedClaims: In the reviewed woody-host guidance, Rosellinia can produce scattered cobwebby whitish mycelia on lower trunks, soil over infected roots, root surfaces, and beneath root-crown or major-root bark.

Removing infected root cortex can expose a whitish fluffy mycelial layer; older mycelium may darken to blackish, brown, or tan and become crustlike, so absence of bright white growth in a late sample does not exclude the organism.

The guidance distinguishes Rosellinia from larger fanlike Armillaria mycelia and from Phytophthora root rot, which does not produce whitish mycelia; these are non-Cannabis differential cues and do not replace crop-linked laboratory confirmation.

Rosellinia can persist in infected root or woody debris and spread through moist soil, supporting conservative soil, water-runoff, tool, and root-debris biosecurity after a confirmed diagnosis; this source does not establish Cannabis treatment efficacy.

sources.title: White root rot
supportedClaims: The institutional cross-crop profile describes mycelial webs and strands near roots, bark invasion with fan-like growth, and white-to-greyish mats beneath bark that accompany progressive root-tissue rot.

The source identifies a broad host range that includes herbaceous plants, but its apple-tree timing, canopy morphology, climate, and control statements must not be transferred as Cannabis thresholds or expected progression.

Its three credited photographs are copyrighted to the State of Queensland and lack item-level automated-training permission; their landing-page metadata may inform capture planning, but no image is copied, displayed, or indexed as Cannabis ground truth.
